title: Raymer Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Raymer wells have a 157-foot median depth, 8.5 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $11,500-$20,600.
h1: Wells and Water in Raymer, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land or building near Raymer means understanding what the local well records actually show. Within 5 miles of New Raymer, Colorado, DWR records list 128 permitted wells. Of those, 76 are recorded as constructed, 88 report a total depth, 30 report a pump yield, and 8 report a static water level.

The local numbers are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. Nearby wells can differ substantially, especially where the records identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Check the permit file, neighboring well construction, water rights, septic layout, and access for the specific parcel before committing to a purchase.

sections.heading: Raymer well depths range from shallow plains wells to deep holes
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Raymer is 157 feet. The middle half of reported wells runs from 80 to 296 feet, so a driller bidding a typical site may be working in that range rather than quoting one fixed depth. The depth distribution is broad: 28% of wells are under 100 feet, 47% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 10% are 300 to 600 feet, and 15% exceed 600 feet.

The deepest reported well reaches 1,545 feet, while the 90th percentile is 1,042 feet. This spread matters on the plains, where alluvium and sedimentary rock can produce very different drilling conditions. A nearby shallow well is useful evidence, but it should not be treated as a promise that your lot will match it.

sections.heading: What Raymer wells produce for household and stock use
sections.html:
Among the 30 Raymer-area records reporting pump yield, the median is 8.5 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 3.9 to 14.5 gallons per minute. The reported mix is 27% at 1 to 5 gpm, 47% at 5 to 15 gpm, and 27% above 15 gpm. No reported well is listed below 1 gpm.

That is generally workable information for a rural buyer, but yield is not the same as storage or water quality. A modest-producing well can still serve a home if the pressure tank and storage plan are designed correctly. Ask for the pumping test and completion report. Household-use exempt wells have a 35 gpm pumping limit, and stock use appears frequently in these permits.

sections.heading: Raymer water levels and what the permit history says
sections.html:
Only 8 wells report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is small. Those records show a median depth to water of 46 feet, with the middle half from 23 to 191 feet. The range suggests that water may be relatively shallow at some sites but substantially deeper at others.

The permit record does not provide enough water-level observations to call a dropping or rising trend. Permit activity itself spans the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2024: 2 permits in the 1950s, 9 in the 1960s, 11 in the 1970s, 12 in the 1980s, 16 in the 1990s, 23 in the 2000s, 12 in the 2010s, and 8 in the 2020s. Use those records as site history, not a basin-wide water-level forecast.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around New Raymer
sections.html:
The most active names in the available permit records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), associated with 19 wells; Kugler Sales & Service (Kugler, Dean L.), associated with 17; and Stewart Drilling Co. (Stewart, Dennis W.), associated with 6. These are record counts, not a recommendation or a guarantee that any driller is available for a new project.

Before requesting bids, pull the completion reports for nearby wells and compare depth, casing, grout, aquifer description, yield, and pump information. The records identify 115 wells in an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, 4 in the Pierre Shale, and 1 in the Laramie-Fox Hills. That local construction history can help a driller explain why bids differ.

sections.heading: A Raymer well budget: drilling versus a finished system
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 157-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $5,500 to $8,600. That is only the drilling portion, not a functioning water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,500 to $20,600 at the median depth. A deep hole can move well beyond that planning range, particularly when casing, grout, difficult formation, pump setting, or extra trenching is required. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Checks that matter before building near Raymer
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk cannot be ruled out from a median alone. The wide local depth range and the number of wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers make lot-specific investigation important. Have the driller review neighboring permits, and confirm how the proposed well location fits the home, driveway, septic system, and reserve area.

Water quality also needs testing. The mapped area includes 51 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. That fact does not prove contamination at your parcel, but it is a reason to test raw well water before relying on it. The records show no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Ask about treatment only after laboratory results identify a need.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Raymer-area lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s neighboring wells, not just the countywide median. A 157-foot typical depth and 8.5 gpm median yield are useful for a preliminary budget, while the 80-to-296-foot middle-half depth range shows why a fixed quote can be misleading. Request DWR permits and construction reports for the closest comparable wells.

Before closing, confirm the permitted use, well location, access for a rig, electrical route, septic setbacks, and the cost of connecting the well to the house. Domestic, household, and stock uses are common in the records, while irrigation accounts for 1%. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask whether an augmentation plan or other water-rights issue affects the intended use. Nearby Weldona, Jackson Lake, Saddle Ridge, Blue Sky, Morgan Heights, and Snyder can provide broader regional context, but the immediate neighboring wells matter most.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Raymer, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of New Raymer is 157 feet, and the middle half runs from 80 to 296 feet. Depth varies widely: 28% are under 100 feet, while 15% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,545 feet, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee a shallow hole on your property.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Raymer?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 157-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $5,500 to $8,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,500 to $20,600. Deeper drilling, difficult formations, casing, and site conditions can increase the final price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Raymer?
faq.a: Among 30 records reporting pump yield, the median is 8.5 gallons per minute, with a middle half from 3.9 to 14.5 gpm. The records show 27% producing 1 to 5 gpm and 47% producing 5 to 15 gpm. No reported well is under 1 gpm, but a pumping test is still essential for a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Raymer, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from permit records alone. There are 51 PFAS sampling or contamination sites mapped within about 10 miles, which makes laboratory testing important before using a well for drinking. The area has no mapped historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test raw water and choose treatment from the results.

faq.q: Are Raymer wells getting deeper or running lower?
faq.a: The available records do not support a reliable water-level trend. Only 8 wells report static water levels; their median depth to water is 46 feet, with a middle half from 23 to 191 feet. Permit dates extend through 2024, but permit counts and the small water-level sample cannot establish that groundwater is dropping or rising.
